stances.claim: CJ Gesmundo 'correctly, IMHO, began by recalling the reforms started by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.' -- endorsing the SPJI as a successor to APJR rather than a stand-alone innovation, and acknowledging CJ Davide's APJR as the 'first structured plan for judicial reform created way back in 2001.'

CJ Davide's APJR was institutionally validated by international aid agencies (World Bank, ADB, USAID, CIDA, JICA), with the World Bank including the APJR on its website 'as a model for developing countries to emulate' -- making the reform's external prestige a matter of documentary record CJ traced in his 536-page 'Judicial Renaissance' (SC Press, Nov. 2006).

CJ Panganiban's own statement of vision-values-goals at the start of his incumbency systematized the judicial reform program: Four Ins (integrity, independence, industry, intelligence); four corroding threats (influence, interference, indifference, insolence); the plague of 'ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship); four ACID problems (limited access, corruption, incompetence, delay); a competent-ethical-lawyer vision; the DHL promise to 26,000 employees (dedication, honesty, loyalty); and two loftier goals -- safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity under the rule of law.

The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity, formed post-retirement, continues the philosophy through professional chairs, legal scholarships, dissertation contests, 'Esmel' fellowships, and the planned Center for Liberty and Prosperity (with interactive Museum in partnership with the SC) and Entrepreneurship Fund -- making the CJ's vision generational rather than tenure-bound.

Beyond Davide and Panganiban, CJ Gesmundo's SPJI launch credits CJ Puno (Writs of Amparo, Habeas Data, Kalikasan -- the great writs of freedom), CJ Corona (Quezon City Courts; Judicial Affidavit Rule precursor), CJ de Castro (Family Courts; Children in Conflict with the Law), CJ Bersamin (Revised Law Student Practice; Mandatory Clinical Legal Education; 2019 amendments to Civil Procedure and Evidence), and CJ Peralta (Continuous Trial). 'Sorry, no mention of Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Four Pillars' -- a pointed omission CJ flags without endorsing.

notable_anecdotes: The two-Monday series structure made explicit -- 'Following his lead, I will take up today these past initiatives, and next Monday, the present and future reform plans' -- establishing this column as installment 1 of the SPJI walkthrough.

CJ's 'Judicial Renaissance' (Supreme Court Press, Nov. 2006) at 536 pages, dedicated to CJ Davide -- including Davide's biographical arc from 'the remote barangay of Colawin in Argao, Cebu' to lawyer, lawmaker, constitution framer, elections chairman, AJ, and CJ -- making the predecessor tribute documentary rather than only ceremonial.
The World Bank including the APJR 'as a model for developing countries to emulate to deserve the Bank's support' -- converting Davide's reform into international institutional currency.

CJ's self-quoted statement of vision-values-goals at incumbency assumption -- the Four Ins / four corroding threats / plague of 'ships' / four ACID problems / lawyer-vision / DHL / loftier goals architecture -- preserved verbatim as the column's self-citation centerpiece, modeling reform-by-acronym pedagogy.

The 'Plague of ships' coinage -- 'kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship' -- a memorable rhyming-suffix mnemonic for institutional capture risks that has stayed in CJ's repeating vocabulary.
The 26,000-employee DHL promise -- 'dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty to the judiciary' -- modeling reform-by-acronym at the staff-engagement level.

The Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity Oct. 18-20, 2006 as the CJ-incumbency capstone -- paired with FLP's post-retirement formation to demonstrate continuity through institutional infrastructure.
The 'Esmel' fellowships -- a named program with a specific moniker -- kept in the FLP roster without explanation, modeling the kind of named-program proliferation institutional reform produces.

CJ Puno credited as 'father of the great writs of freedom' -- and the three writs named (Amparo, Habeas Data, Kalikasan) preserved verbatim -- making Puno's institutional fatherhood a quotable formula.

The Sereno omission: 'Sorry, no mention of Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Four Pillars' -- CJ pointedly flagging her absence from Gesmundo's tribute roster without himself filling in the substantive Four Pillars detail -- a delicate institutional move that registers the omission while respecting the SC's institutional position.

The post-Dec. 7, 2006 epistemic-limit acknowledgment -- 'I do not have the details of these remedial reforms undertaken after my term' -- and reader-referral to pio.sc@judiciary.gov.ph, modeling honest disclosure of knowledge boundaries.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his two-Monday series on the Supreme Court's 'Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027' (SPJI) by 'reminiscing the past' as CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo himself did at launch. Gesmundo, CJ writes, 'correctly, IMHO, began by recalling the reforms started by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.' -- whose 'Action Program for Judicial Reform' (APJR) Gesmundo praised as 'the first structured plan for judicial reform created way back in 2001... a truly impressive plan from which (were) drawn some of (the) present activities in the SPJI.' CJ recounts that in his 536-page 'Judicial Renaissance' (Supreme Court Press, November 2006) -- dedicated to CJ Davide and available in the SC Library -- he traced Davide's 'modest roots from the remote barangay of Colawin in Argao, Cebu' to his career as lawyer, lawmaker, constitution framer, elections chairman, associate justice, and chief justice, and tracked the support the APJR drew from the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, USAID, Canadian International Development Agency, and Japan International Cooperation Agency -- the World Bank including the APJR on its website 'as a model for developing countries to emulate.' Prior to Davide's December 20, 2005 retirement, the SC held the International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms on November 28-30, 2005. CJ thanks Gesmundo for crediting him with 'egalitarian justice' through 'institutionalizing the perspective of law and economics as an essential element of his Liberty and Prosperity Programs,' then 'in all modesty' lays out his own statement of vision-values-goals from incumbency assumption: 'I vow to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- one that is morally courageous to resist influence, interference, indifference, and insolence. I envision a judiciary that is impervious to the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.' He pledged to strengthen the APJR with focus on the 'four ACID problems that corrode justice in our country: (1) limited access to justice by the poor, (2) corruption, (3) incompetence, and (4) delay in the delivery of quality justice'; sought 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, and morally upright'; promised to grant maximum benefits to 26,000 judicial employees in exchange for DHL -- 'dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty to the judiciary'; with all leading to 'safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people under the rule of law.' His incumbency capstone was the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity on October 18-20, 2006; after retirement on December 7, 2006, the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity was formed to continue the philosophy via professional chairs, legal scholarships, dissertation contests, and 'Esmel' fellowships, with ultimate projects of a Center for Liberty and Prosperity housing an interactive Museum in partnership with the SC, and an 'Entrepreneurship Fund.' Gesmundo also hailed CJ Reynato S. Puno as 'father of the great writs of freedom -- the Writ of Amparo, Writ of Habeas Data, and Writ of Kalikasan,' and cited Rules-of-Court amendments by CJ Renato C. Corona (Quezon City Courts and Judicial Affidavit Rule precursor), CJ Teresita Leonardo de Castro (Family Courts and Children in Conflict with the Law), CJ Lucas P. Bersamin (Revised Law Student Practice, Mandatory Clinical Legal Education, 2019 Amendments to Rules of Civil Procedure and on Evidence), and CJ Diosdado M. Peralta (Continuous Trial, 'among others'). CJ closes pointedly: 'Sorry, no mention of Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Four Pillars' -- and acknowledges his epistemic limit, having retired December 7, 2006, referring readers to pio.sc@judiciary.gov.ph for details on post-term reforms now embedded in the Rules of Court.
